title: Nature loves change
hook: nothing is more natural than change, Marcus writes (Meditations 4.36)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said you don't need the seaside to get away: you can step back into your own mind at any hour. Your line was the inner retreat. Did you take one, even for a minute? Day one hundred eighty-eight.

Find an old photo of yourself. Ten years old, maybe, squinting at the camera. Most of the cells in that face have long since been replaced. The haircut is gone, the house may be gone, the people holding the camera may be gone. And still, when a gray hair shows up, or a favorite café closes, or a friend moves across the country, something in us says: this isn't supposed to happen. We treat change like a malfunction. An emperor sitting in a tent by a cold river, nearly two thousand years ago, wrote a note to himself about exactly that feeling. Today: nature loves change.
screen: `AN OLD PHOTO OF YOU.` → `CHANGE FEELS LIKE A MALFUNCTION.` → `NATURE LOVES CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180, and much of that time he spent on campaign along the Danube. At night he wrote private notes in Greek, never meant for us. We call them the Meditations. In Book Four he tells himself to keep watching how everything comes about through change, and then he adds a surprising line. In George Long's old translation, the nature of the universe "loves nothing so much as to change the things which are and to make new things like them." Notice the word loves. Marcus doesn't say nature puts up with change, or suffers it. Change is what nature most enjoys doing. The things that exist now, he goes on, are seeds of what will come from them. Marcus admired Heraclitus, the older Greek thinker remembered for saying that everything flows. And later, in Book Seven, Marcus makes it ordinary. Are you afraid of change? Nothing can happen without it. You can't take a warm bath unless the wood changes in the fire. You can't eat unless the food changes in you. The very things that keep you alive are changes. So Marcus isn't asking himself to like every loss. He lost several children, and his notes are not cold about it. He's asking something smaller and harder: to stop treating change as an insult, as if the universe had broken its promise. It never promised to stay still. Your line for today: change is natural.
screen: `NOTES FROM A TENT BY THE DANUBE.` · `IT LOVES NOTHING SO MUCH AS TO CHANGE.` · `THE BATH NEEDS THE WOOD TO BURN.` · then, large: `CHANGE IS NATURAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing changing. Settle where you are. Pick something small and close: your breath going in and out, the light on the wall, a sound that rises and fades, the warmth of your hands. Just watch it change. You don't have to fix it or hold it. If a bigger change in your life comes to mind, let it sit beside the small one for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Nature loves change. Marcus wrote that the universe loves nothing so much as changing what is and making new things like it. Today's word.
Your line: change is natural. Today, when something shifts that you didn't ask for, say the line once before you react. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often keep a short line like this one in view, and some make a habit of pausing to notice change in small things, such as the breath or the light, as Marcus advised himself.

fork.setup: you're Marcus. you've noticed you're afraid of change. what do you write to yourself?

fork.reveal: in Book Seven he asks who is afraid of change, and points out that even a bath needs the wood to change in the fire.

original.note: Greek, the language Marcus wrote in: change, a turning into something else. the Stoics used it for the constant change of nature.

trapdoor: what you thought: change is something that goes wrong.
what it means: for Marcus, change is what nature most loves to do.
what a scholar hears: the Stoic picture of a universe always remaking itself, with Heraclitus's flowing river behind it.

notes: Check the Long 1862 wording of 4.36 exactly: 'the nature of the universe loves nothing so much as to change the things which are and to make new things like them.'
7.18 paraphrase (bath needs the wood to change; food must change to nourish): confirm the passage number.
'Everything flows' (panta rhei) is attributed to Heraclitus by later sources, not preserved in his own words. The script says he is 'remembered for saying'. Confirm the hedge.
Marcus's children: several died young; confirm the phrasing 'He lost several children'.

Book Four setting: tradition holds parts of the Meditations were written on campaign; Book Two is headed 'among the Quadi', Book Three 'at Carnuntum'. The hook's 'tent by a cold river' is an image, not a claim about Book Four's location. Confirm it reads that way.
Hook softened from 'every cell in that face has been replaced' (a popular myth; some cells, such as many neurons and the lens of the eye, last a lifetime) to 'most of the cells'. Confirm.
